content: Cholera is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Individuals can contract cholera by consuming contaminated food or water. This contamination often occurs when cholera bacteria are introduced into drinking water or water used for growing or preparing food. Additionally, the disease can spread when fecal matter from sewage contaminates the water supply. Most people infected with cholera experience mild or no symptoms. However, approximately 1 in 10 individuals with cholera will develop severe symptoms. These symptoms include profuse watery diarrhea, often described as rice-water stools, increased thirst, leg cramps, and restlessness or irritability. In severe cases, cholera can lead to significant dehydration, which may result in kidney failure and death if not promptly treated. Who is at risk? Individuals living in or traveling to areas where cholera is endemic are at the highest risk of contracting the disease. While cholera in travelers is rare, it can occur in specific situations, such as among those visiting friends or family in affected regions, healthcare workers, or response workers in outbreak settings. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identifies several countries with active cholera transmission. These include: Africa: Burundi, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Somalia, South Africa, South Sudan, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe. Asia: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines. Middle East: Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, Yemen. Americas: Dominican Republic, Haiti. Pacific: No active transmission reported. For detailed information on cholera transmission levels and affected areas within specific countries, consult the cholera section on the destination page of the CDC's travel website. How can travelers prevent cholera? Travelers can protect themselves from cholera by taking the following precautions: 1. Choose safer food and drinks: Follow food and drink safety guidelines to minimize the risk of consuming contaminated items. 2. Wash hands frequently: Use soap and water to wash hands regularly. If soap and water are unavailable, use hand sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol. Avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth unless your hands are clean. When coughing or sneezing, cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your sleeve, not your hands. How is cholera treated? The cornerstone of cholera treatment is rehydration. Patients should drink plenty of fluids to replace lost electrolytes. Those with severe dehydration may require intravenous (IV) fluids. Antibiotics are recommended for individuals who are severely ill or at risk of becoming severely ill, such as pregnant individuals and children. Zinc supplementation has also been shown to improve cholera symptoms in children aged 3 to 14 years and to reduce the duration of acute diarrhea in children older than six months.
